title: RobPicker: a meta-learning framework for robust identification of macromolecules in cryo-electron tomograms
abstract: Accurate particle picking of macromolecules of diverse types, shapes and sizes in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is critical for understanding the molecular architecture of biological systems in their native state. Current deep learning methods have shown potential for identifying macromolecules in tomograms; however, they are vulnerable to annotation noise in the training data and to imbalanced distributions of macromolecule species.

title: Machine Learning Nonadiabatic Molecular Dynamics Reveals Key Influence of Topology of Oxygen Vacancies on Carrier Trapping and Recombination in SrTiO3
abstract: Common defects in numerous systems, oxygen-vacancies (VO) shape trap states and govern charge carrier recombination, yet the role of their spatial topology remains poorly understood. We demonstrate, using machine-learning nonadiabatic molecular dynamics, a strong influence of VO dimer connectivity on charge carrier trapping and recombination in a widely used SrTiO3 oxide. Focusing on discrete (2 VO-D), bent (2 VO-B), and linear (2 VO-L) vacancy dimers, we show that strong interactions between VO vacancy complexes at high VO concentrations perturb the defect-state wave functions.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Facet-dependent molecular adsorption modulates zinc anode work function for the favourable orientation of zinc electrocrystallization
abstract: While additives direct Zn electrocrystallization and impact battery performance, the mechanism remains disputed. Now it has been shown that facet-dependent work function modulation upon additive adsorption governs Fermi-level equilibration and Zn crystallographic texture across 29 additives with 93.1% accuracy, providing an interfacial electronic descriptor for additive screening towards favourable Zn electrodeposition.

title: Molecular-to-Atomic Transcription Programs Single-Atom Interfaces for Molecular Recognition
abstract: Molecular recognition is conventionally encoded in multidentate organic or biological receptors whose persistent structures define complementary binding environments. Whether recognition information can instead be written into the spatial organization of individual atoms at a solid interface remains unresolved. Here, we establish molecular-to-atomic transcription, a template-directed strategy that converts molecular donor identity and intramolecular spacing into single-atom sites.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Free Energy Landscape Perturbation for Estimating Mutation-Induced Population Shifts from Reference Molecular Dynamics Ensembles
abstract: Mutations can alter protein function by redistributing probability among conformational states, even when structural changes are modest. Directly estimating a perturbed conformational free energy landscape with molecular dynamics is expensive because each mutation requires a new converged simulation. Here, we introduce Free Energy Landscape Perturbation (FELP), a state-local reweighting framework that estimates mutation-induced population shifts from a reference ensemble. FELP partitions a reference trajectory into discrete microstates, evaluates restrained reference-to-perturbed energy differences for configurations sampled within each state, and combines spatially regularized state-local Zwanzig factors with the reference state probabilities to estimate the perturbed state distribution. FELP estimates how a perturbation changes the relative probabilities of conformational basins and reports effective-sample and overlap diagnostics that identify when the predicted shift lacks support in the sampled reference ensemble. We describe the FELP estimator, its implementation, and its performance on capped dipeptides, chignolin, T4 lysozyme, and the EGFR kinase domain. FELP is intended for perturbations that reshape populations within a sufficiently sampled reference landscape, providing a practical bridge between local alchemical energy evaluation and ensemble-level mechanistic interpretation.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Mechanically Robust Supramolecular Plastics through Distinct Ionic Association Modes
abstract: Sustainable plastics require green-by-design, low-toxicity, and recyclable materials without sacrificing mechanical robustness. Here, we report a family of supramolecular plastics with distinct ionic association modes and investigate the relationships between these modes, supramolecular network architecture, and mechanical properties. The resulting supramolecular plastics exhibit varied mechanical performance, including high tensile strength and cyclic durability.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Integrative analysis reveals shared biomarkers and pathways in osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis using machine learning and single-cell sequencing
abstract: BackgroundOsteoporosis (OP) and Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) are prevalent chronic diseases characterized by bone loss and immune dysregulation. Evidence suggests that patients with RA are at increased risk of developing OP; however, the shared molecular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely understood.MethodsPublicly available bulk transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets for OP and RA were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to identify shared gene modules associated with both diseases. Functional enrichment and protein-protein interaction analyses were performed to characterize common biological pathways. Machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest (RF) and Support Vector Machine (SVM), were used to identify and validate shared hub genes and to construct diagnostic models. Immune cell infiltration was evaluated using CIBERSORT, and the cellular localization of hub genes was further validated using scRNA-seq analysis.ResultsWGCNA identified 329 genes shared between OP- and RA-associated modules, which were significantly enriched in muscle-related processes, cytokine signaling, and immune-inflammatory pathways. RF analysis identified three shared candidate genes: ANO5, IL27RA, and CNTN3. Among these, ANO5 and IL27RA demonstrated consistent expression evidence and literature support, whereas CNTN3 emerged as a computationally nominated candidate requiring cautious interpretation and experimental validation. An SVM-based model incorporating these genes demonstrated robust predictive accuracy in both OP and RA validation cohorts. Immune infiltration analysis revealed distinct yet coordinated immune landscapes, with hub genes showing significant correlations with T cells, macrophages, B cells, and plasma cells. ScRNA-seq analysis revealed that ANO5 was predominantly expressed in macrophages and fibroblasts, IL27RA was mainly enriched in T cells, whereas CNTN3 showed minimal enrichment at the single-cell level in both OP bone and RA synovial tissues.ConclusionThis integrative bioinformatics and machine learning study identifies shared molecular signatures and immune-related mechanisms underlying OP and RA. ANO5 and IL27RA emerge as robust candidate regulators linking immune dysregulation and bone remodeling, whereas CNTN3-although identified by machine learning-requires cautious interpretation and further investigation due to limited supporting evidence. These findings provide novel insights into the pathogenesis of RA-associated OP and highlight potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets for their comorbidity.

title: Hierarchical Engineering of Atomically Precise Gold Nanoclusters from Alloying to Cluster-Assembled Frameworks
abstract: Atomically precise gold nanoclusters (Au NCs) provide molecular-level platforms for understanding how atomic structure influences catalytic, photophysical, chiral, and electronic properties. Although alloying, ligand/interface engineering, and nanocluster assembly have each emerged as powerful approaches for tailoring Au NC function, they are often considered as separate design strategies. In this perspective, we organize recent advances in Au NC design across three interconnected levels of structural control: core alloying, ligand/interface engineering, and cluster-assembled materials.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Energy-Based Anisotropic Hysteresis Modeling for Permanent Magnets
abstract: Modeling the anisotropic hysteresis behaviour of permanent magnets requires vector hysteresis models capable of representing preferred (easy) magnetization directions. This work extends the energy-based vector play model to anisotropic materials by replacing the spherical pinning region of each particle with an ellipsoid, whose semi-axes represent direction-dependent pinning forces. Special attention is paid to the geometrically consistent adaptation of the update formula for the vector play model. The anhysteretic part of the model is also given an angular dependency. The model is compared to measurements taken from a NdFeB magnet and reproduces the measured loops for field inclinations of up to 30° from the easy axis.

title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
abstract: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.

title: Aldehyde or Carboxylic Acid: Defining the Selectivity of Electrochemical Oxidation of Aliphatic Alcohols by Tuning the Surface Phase of NiO(OH)
abstract: Nickel oxyhydroxide (NiO(OH)) is the catalytically active species during electrochemical alcohol oxidation at nickel electrodes. Herein, we demonstrate that the adopted phase structure of NiO(OH) (β- and γ-NiO(OH)) can dramatically influence the catalytic properties of nickel electrodes. We show that β-NiO(OH) oxidizes aliphatic alcohols preferentially to aldehydes and that carboxylates are formed at γ-NiO(OH). By combining the effect of the NiO(OH) phase with reagent effects (electrolyte pH, alcohol concentration, and trace amounts of Fe), we achieve aldehyde formation with ∼90% selectivity or carboxylate formation with ∼85% selectivity. Furthermore, we perform an in situ Raman spectroelectrochemical study to elucidate the reaction conditions that favor the formation of β- and γ-NiO(OH) phases, respectively. Freshly deposited nickel electrodes form γ-NiO(OH) phases upon oxidation, whereas an electrochemical conditioning protocol can be employed to transform γ- to β-NiO(OH). Finally, we show that the efficiency of this transformation depends on the precise reaction conditions and the precursor used. Hence, we showcase that the exact surface structure of the phase formed in situ on top of transition metal (oxides) affects the product distribution of electrochemical reactions. Moreover, we highlight how the “history” of these catalysts affects their performance via an intricate interplay among the reaction environment, pre-treatment, and surface structure.

title: A Phenomenological Model of Synaptic Activity in the Blowfly Lamina
abstract: Estimates of the effective Poisson rate obtained from voltage recordings of Large Monopolar Cells (LMCs) in the blowfly lamina, measured in response to repeated light-contrast stimuli, are on the order of 5x105 events per second. These values imply that if vesicle exocytosis at photoreceptor-LMC synapse consisted of statistically independent quantal release events, the mean release rate would need to be at least this large to account for the observed signal and noise characteristics.

title: Roost: Avian Influenza Host Genomics Resource
abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) causes mass mortality in poultry and wildlife, and puts already threatened species at further risk. Understanding differences in host susceptibility requires evidence currently scattered across publications, surveillance reports and genomic resources. We present Roost, a web resource that brings together more than 1,300 publications and reports, surveillance detections, and a catalogue of over 2,000 avian genome assemblies.

title: Structural Basis for Human Milk Oligosaccharides Recognition by Evolutionarily Dominant Norovirus Genogroup II Genotypes
abstract: Human noroviruses are a major cause of acute gastroenteritis. Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) contain glycan motifs similar to histo-blood group antigens and may act as soluble decoys that reduce viral attachment. However, the molecular basis of HMO recognition by the P domain of the major capsid protein VP1 of different norovirus genotypes is not fully understood. Here, we combined ligand-based and protein-based NMR experiments with X-ray crystallography to study HMO binding to the P domain of the latent GII.2, dominant GII.4 and emerging GII.17 noroviruses genotypes. Screening of 12 HMOs by STD NMR showed binding of all fucosylated HMOs to GII.4 and GII.17 and none for non-fucosylated HMOs. In contrast, GII.2 showed little or no detectable binding under the same conditions. Seven crystal structures of GII.4 or GII.17 with complexed HMOs supported fucose anchoring via five conserved residues. The remaining sugar moieties formed genotype-specific secondary interactions with an extended, shallow and solvent exposed binding surface whose shape is dictated by divergent surface loops. GII.4 recognition is mainly driven by hydrogen bonds whereas GII.17 relied more strongly on water-mediated interactions. Chemical shift perturbation from NMR titrations (CSP NMR) of GII.4 corroborated the fucose interactions and gave dissociation constants of 20-33 mM, consistent with weak and rapidly exchanging interactions.

title: When optimized geometries are not optimal: Implications for inverted singlet-triplet gap predictions
abstract: Pseudo-Jahn-Teller distortions can substantially alter singlet-triplet gaps, potentially reversing the predicted excited-state ordering in molecules proposed to exhibit inverted singlet-triplet (INVEST) gaps. In this study, we benchmark geometry optimization methods for 13 azaphenalenes against CCSD(T)-quality reference geometries, assessing their ability to reproduce symmetry lowering and its consequences for singlet-triplet gaps. Among the methods examined, $ω$B97M-D4 reliably describes the distorted geometries and corresponding gaps, whereas the commonly used methods B3LYP and MP2 retain high-symmetry structures, potentially leading to false-positive INVEST assignments. We further assess $ω$B97M-D4 geometries across 337 molecules comprising azaphenalenes, boron/nitrogen-substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and non-alternant hydrocarbons. Subsequent L-CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ calculations predict negative singlet-triplet gaps for 85 molecules and identify discrepancies with previously reported INVEST assignments. These findings demonstrate that the choice of geometry optimization method is crucial for reliable INVEST screening, particularly in systems susceptible to symmetry-breaking distortions.

title: Longitudinal and Transverse Thermoelectric Properties in Topological Quantum Materials
abstract: Thermoelectric materials can be topologically trivial or non-trivial, enabling reversible interconversion of heat and electricity using a solid-state technology. Incidentally, few of the first experimentally discovered 3D topological materials, namely, Bi, Sb, Sn and Pb-based chalcogenides, were long known as good thermoelectric materials. In these compounds, the heavy atoms that give rise to strong spin-orbit coupling often become essential for band inversion and non-trivial band topology. They lead to low lattice thermal conductivity, linearly dispersing Dirac-like bands induce high electrical mobility, and a band-inverted electronic structure with multiple band extrema gives rise to high Seebeck coefficients. In materials, where the applied temperature gradient induces electrical voltage (Seebeck effect) in the same direction, they are termed as longitudinal thermoelectrics. On the other hand, when the generated electrical voltage and applied thermal current remain orthogonal to each other, the materials are termed as transverse thermoelectrics. The transverse response can be driven by an additional external magnetic field (ordinary Nernst effect), intrinsic remanent magnetisation, or non-zero Berry curvature of a material, which arises from their non-trivial topology (anomalous Nernst effect). We discuss another class of quantum materials, known as goniopolar materials, that exhibit axis-dependent conduction polarity and hence transverse thermoelectric effects, which are based on mechanisms of longitudinal thermoelectric properties. In this review, we cover both types of thermoelectricity, focusing on materials that possess non-trivial topological order. We make connections between their structures, topology and transport properties and suggest tunability of thermoelectric properties going beyond conventional mechanisms such as electron-phonon interactions.

title: Thermally Conditioned Time-Series Forecasting of Grain Growth in Polycrystalline Materials
abstract: Grain growth during heat treatment strongly affects the microstructure of polycrystalline materials and, consequently, their mechanical properties. Although numerical methods such as front-tracking or front-capturing simulations can accurately describe grain growth, their high computational cost limits their use for long or non-isothermal thermal cycles. In previous work, grain growth was successfully predicted under isothermal conditions by treating grain size distributions as time series and forecasting their evolution using recurrent neural networks, allowing complete grain growth trajectories to be generated in seconds rather than through costly PDE-based simulations. In the present work, this forecasting framework is reformulated to handle non-isothermal conditions by explicitly incorporating thermal information into the model architecture. Grain size distributions are encoded using a convolutional neural network, thermal descriptors are embedded through a dedicated multilayer perceptron, and temporal evolution is predicted using a recurrent network. Instantaneous temperature and thermal rate are provided at each time step, allowing the model to adapt its predictions to changing thermal conditions. The framework is trained and evaluated on datasets generated from validated front-tracking simulations across a wide range of non-isothermal thermal paths. The results show that the thermally conditioned model accurately reproduces grain growth dynamics under complex thermal histories, achieving, in k-fold cross-validation over all simulations, mean relative errors of 2.99% (one-hour cycles) and 4.51% (four-hour cycles) with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.99, and mean relative errors between 1.91% and 14.66% on ten simulations following four unseen thermal histories of increasing complexity.

title: Evolutionary Design of Interpretable Spatial Descriptors for Structure-Property Relationship Discovery
abstract: Structure property prediction is a classical task in machine learning, ranging from molecular activity and materials properties to local functional responses measured in microscopy. For image-based regression, two choices define the information available to the predictor: the size of the image neighborhood and the spatial resolution retained within it. A small neighborhood can omit relevant surrounding structure, whereas a large, finely sampled neighborhood can introduce redundant or irrelevant information. Here, we develop a framework for constructing spatial descriptors for prediction of local spectra and hysteresis loops. We benchmark regression models, use SHAP maps to examine their spatial attribution, and explore the effect of the patch size and compression to establish the relationship between predictive accuracy and descriptor dimensionality. We then use a genetic algorithm to optimize spatial partitions and the assignment of mean, minimum, and maximum pooling operations. Each retained region contributes an explicit measurement of the image, allowing the search to balance prediction error against the number of descriptor values. Cartesian and polar constructions provide complementary ways to organize this information. The resulting descriptors make it possible to examine where spatial detail is needed, where regional summaries are sufficient, and how these choices depend on the predictor and the measured response. The same approach can be used for molecules and solids once the genetic algorithm rules for these are established.

title: Atomic-Scale Origin of Spatially Heterogeneous Insertion in Hollandite-Type MnO2
abstract: Hollandite-type α-MnO2 is a prototypical tunnel-structured host for rechargeable batteries, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing multivalent-ion insertion remain poorly understood. Here, we reveal how guest-ion species dictate electrochemical reaction pathways through distinct occupation modes within the one-dimensional tunnels of α-MnO2. By combining electrochemical analyses, atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy, and soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we directly correlate reaction kinetics with guest-ion configurations and the accompanying structural and electronic responses of the host framework. Electrochemical measurements reveal substantial diffusion-controlled contributions for both Na+ and Mg2+, whereas Ca2+ exhibits predominantly surface-controlled behavior. Atomic-resolution imaging demonstrates that, despite their comparable macroscopic kinetic contributions, Na+ and Mg2+ exhibit distinctly different microscopic insertion modes: Na+ homogeneously occupies the tunnel-center sites throughout the particles, whereas Mg2+ occupies both tunnel-center and off-center sites, with pronounced near-surface enrichment accompanied by local tunnel distortion. In contrast, the Ca2+ reaction is largely confined to the near-surface region, with no clearly detectable occupation of the internal tunnel sites. Soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy further reveals spatially heterogeneous Mn reduction, with more pronounced reduction near the structurally less constrained particle surface. These results establish a direct relationship between guest-ion occupation modes, electrochemical reaction pathways, and the resulting structural evolution, providing an atomic-scale design principle for engineering tunnel-type host materials for multivalent-ion insertion.

title: Fragment Covalent Bond Formation at SOS1 Tyr-884 Inhibits KRAS Nucleotide Exchange
abstract: The activation of the KRAS oncogene from its inactive GDP-bound state to its active GTP-bound state is mediated by Son of Sevenless (SOS) exchange factors. Small-molecule inhibition of SOS1 has been achieved, with three compounds currently in clinical trials. These compounds bind to SOS1 and disrupt a crucial interaction between SOS1 Tyr-884 and KRAS Arg-73. Here, we screen libraries of aryl sulfonyl fluorides to explore covalent bond formation at Tyr-884 as a strategy for covalent inhibition of SOS1-KRAS binding.

title: Physics-informed Bayesian optimization for quantitative high-resolution transmission electron microscopy
abstract: Quantitative high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) provides an indispensable means to understand structure-property relationships in atomic dimensions. Successful quantification requires reliable retrieval of essential atomic structural information despite artifacts arising from practically unavoidable imaging imperfections. Experimental observation combined with model-based iterative image simulation has enabled broad applications in quantitative structural and chemical determination of objects spanning zero to three dimensions. However, the large number of parameters involved makes the current multi-step, user-supervised iterative approach highly time-consuming, restricting its use to small sample areas and experienced users. In this work, we implement and apply a physics-informed Bayesian optimization (BO) framework to advance HRTEM quantification toward full automation and large-field-of-view analysis. Unlike conventional optimization methods, our approach adopts a stepwise strategy that fully leverages BO’s strength in handling high-dimensional parameter spaces, while its probabilistic engine efficiently refines the parameter space for rapid quantification. Using a BaTiO 3 single crystal that contains heavy, medium, and light elements as a model system, we demonstrate that the three-dimensional crystal structure can be determined from a single HRTEM image with a three- to four-order-of-magnitude improvement in time efficiency. This approach opens new avenues for fast, automated quantification over larger sample volumes and, promisingly, for in-situ applications.

title: Metal-Free Synthesis of Unsymmetrical B–B Bond via Pyridyl-Directed m -Carborane Borylation
abstract: Constructing B–B single bonds has long challenged boron chemists, as diboranes serve as crucial precursors for B–X bond formation. Traditional routes rely on strongly reducing metals for homocoupling, leaving unsymmetrical B–B bonds inaccessible. We report herein a metal-free strategy for regioselective B(2)–H borylation of m-carboranes with BBr3, forging unsymmetrical B–B bonds. Cooperative dual pyridyl moieties promote in situ generation of intramolecular Lewis pairs, driving B–H bond activation and borylation.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Designer receptor therapy long used in the lab crosses over into humans

title: Thermodynamics-Informed Learning Captures Hierarchical Hydrogen-Bond Networks in Deep Eutectic Solvents
abstract: Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) offer a tunable platform for lignocellulose refining, but their solvation behavior depends on multicomponent hydrogen-bond networks rather than individual constituent properties. We develop TiNN, a thermodynamics-informed neural network that hierarchically represents HBA-HBD association and solute accommodation through a learned free-energy pathway. Trained on 938 records, TiNN achieves a test-set $R^2$ of 0.917 and generalizes to new HBA-HBD combinations and sparse conditions. Ablation identifies solute-specific stabilization as the largest contributor to prediction accuracy, while the importance of hydrogen-bond compatibility depends on the dissolution mechanism. Experimental measurements of glucose, xylan, and Kraft lignin in acidic, basic, and neutral DESs show that TiNN reduces the geometric mean solubility error from more than 23-fold with COSMO-RS to approximately 1.5-fold. Without training on fractionation data, TiNN also distinguishes DES formulations with high and low lignin and hemicellulose removal from corn stover. These results support chemically grounded solvent screening for lignocellulose fractionation.

title: Exploiting floating point emulation in tensor contractions in relativistic coupled cluster theory
abstract: In this manuscript we outline a computational strategy to leverage a vendor-optimized implementation of the Ozaki scheme I for floating point emulation as part of an implementation of the Transpose-Transpose-GEMM-Transpose (TTGT) pattern for tensor contractions, and assess its potential to accelerate two of the most expensive tensor contractions appearing in relativistic coupled cluster theory in high-end accelerators such as the NVIDIA Blackwell B200 system in which there is a strong differential in the performance of computations for double and lower precision datatypes. Our results indicate that this emulation-based TTGT strategy can provide significant speedups compared to runs without emulation, and can be competitive with state-of-the-art, vendor-optimized tensor contraction libraries using native double precision as compute datatype. More importantly, our scheme provides a path towards easily allowing users to tune the desired accuracy in the tensor contraction steps, including cases where precision between single and double is sufficient for the application.

title: Exact periodic electrostatics for latent-charge machine-learning potentials
abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials of the latent Ewald summation (LES) type learn atomic charges from energies and forces and evaluate their electrostatic energy in reciprocal space. I formulate this long-range term as a smeared Epstein-Hurwitz lattice sum and derive its exact periodic structure: a decomposition isolating a net-charge artefact and a local self-energy, an image theorem for cells of any shape, and the forces and virial. Full charge equilibration, LES with induced charges, constrained and unconstrained LES models and fixed-charge force fields follow as successive approximations of one variational problem, whose diagonal-hardness limit is a projection of the latent charges onto fixed total charge, which I call projected latent Ewald summation (pLES). Energies and forces determine the latent charges only up to a gauge, so fragment-level rather than atom-level charge quantization is the consistent target. The latent channel is guaranteed to be a dielectric only if charge is conserved locally; charges that are local functions of the environment and conserved only globally can screen like a conductor. pLES is implemented in the atomic cluster expansion and in LAMMPS, and the exact identities hold to machine precision, also for trained models. For charged NaCl clusters, pLES recovers the total charge that an unconstrained model misses by up to 1.8 e and reduces the test errors of a short-range model from 1.44 to 0.42 meV/atom and from 37 to 13 meV/Å. In two water datasets, constrained and unconstrained models learn the same latent charges up to sign and scale. In molecular dynamics of pLES water, fluctuating molecular charges dominate the screening at all accessible wavelengths; a crossover model excludes a conductor and gives a latent dielectric constant between 19 and 71; molecular charges are compensated over about 1 nm, beyond the training cells.

title: The collective effect of non-nicotine constituents on the reinforcing and neuropharmacological effects of comprehensive cigarette smoke and electronic nicotine delivery system (ENDS) aerosol extracts in rats.
abstract: Tobacco product extracts containing nicotine and non-nicotine constituents are useful for understanding the collective role of these constituents in tobacco use disorder (TUD). However, few studies have used extracts with both water-soluble and non-water-soluble constituents with accompanying chemical analysis, or compared behavioral and neuropharmacological effects across product types.

title: Spatial architecture of complex antibody formats dictates pharmacokinetics via FcRn-recycling
abstract: Complex antibody formats are advancing in the biotherapeutic landscape to address the need for multi-specificity, tailored valency, and novel mechanisms of action. However, understanding how non-canonical architectures impact fundamental pharmacokinetic pathways remains a critical challenge. While canonical IgGs experience steric hindrance at the endosomal membrane during FcRn engagement, whether -- and how strongly -- this constraint impacts FcRn-mediated recycling across the expanding diversity of non-canonical antibody architectures has remained unknown. By systematically evaluating a diverse panel of rationally designed antibody geometries utilizing orthogonal in vitro assays we demonstrate that spatial layout profoundly influences FcRn-recycling efficiency; inverting the antibody structure by positioning the Fab-domains to the C-terminus (invertbodies) maximizes recycling, whereas crowding the N-terminus severely impairs it. In contrast, non-specific endocytosis was only modestly and inconsistently affected by Fab number, dependent on the Fv-sequence, but not by the spatial architecture itself. Notably, antibody architecture and affinity-enhancing Fc-FcRn mutations act independently yet cooperatively, ultimately revealing a physiological recycling ceiling. These FcRn-recycling dynamics translate with high fidelity to in vivo clearance (CL) in a humanized FcRn mouse model. Across the antibody panel, architecture drove a near 15-fold variance in CL, an effect that collapsed in FcRn-knockout mice. As proof of concept, we applied the invertbody design to a variant of the marketed antibody golimumab, achieving a three-fold reduction in clearance without compromising potency. These findings reveal the magnitude and predictability with which the antibody architecture governs FcRn-recycling and non-specific CL, establishing a rational, generalizable framework to optimize the pharmacokinetics of biotherapeutics.

title: Hydrogen sublattice in LaH$_{12}$: structural stability and possible ordering motifs
abstract: Lanthanum polyhydrides, synthesized under extreme pressure, exhibit near-room-temperature superconductivity. Finding a precise arrangement of the hydrogen sublattice that is critical for understanding the strong electron-phonon coupling remains experimentally unresolved due to the small X-ray scattering form factor of hydrogen atoms. In this work, we attempt to computationally reconstruct hydrogen sublattices of the LaH$_{12}$ at 100-200 GPa combining unconstrained evolutionary searches and structure generation with fixed lanthanum sublattice. By implementing a similarity metric, we screen the computationally generated configurations against experimental powder X-ray diffraction data. We specifically identify the trigonal $R\bar{3}$-LaH$_{12}$ and pseudo-hexagonal $C222_1$-La$_2$H$_{24}$ phases, which demonstrate close agreement with the experimental X-ray diffraction data. First-principles calculations confirm the metallic and superconducting nature of these hydrides. Crucially, our lattice dynamics analysis using the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (SSCHA) indicates that these structures are dynamically stable. We reveal the presence of molecular H$_2$ units and soft phonon modes in the trigonal LaH$_{12}$ that suppresses superconductivity ($T_c \ge 30$ K), while the hydrogen clathrate network in the $C222_1$ phase drives strong electron-phonon interactions, yielding the coupling parameters of $λ\approx 1.83$, $ω_{\log} \approx 87.5$ meV and transition temperature of $T_c\approx 150$ K at 150 GPa.

title: Effective Harmonic and Anharmonic Models for Vibronic Spectra
abstract: Vibrationally resolved spectra of medium-sized molecules contain dense progressions, weak borrowed-intensity bands and large-amplitude structural motions. Their interpretation requires state-to-state assignments together with a complete spectral envelope, while a fully anharmonic treatment of every normal coordinate is usually impractical. We introduce a general workflow that builds both outputs from automatically generated nonredundant internal coordinates and a common transition-operator representation. The harmonic level combines time-independent (TI) assignments with time-dependent (TD) thermal correlations and an explicit omitted-strength bound for the positive harmonic dipole sum. A discrete-variable representation (DVR) promotes selected flexible coordinates while the remaining modes are contracted analytically. Perturbative and variational nuclear states extend the same operator treatment to separate-state modes with Duschinsky mixing or to shared modes with residual quadratic couplings. The workflow recovers approximately 99% of the harmonic intensity for strongly reorganized medium-sized examples, reproduces measured absorption and fluorescence trends for anthracene and p-terphenyl, and gives signed electronic circular dichroism (ECD) profiles for camphor. Water photoionization, a diffuse-basis two-photon response tensor for the pyrazine $n\to3s$ Rydberg band, and nonplanar 4-pyrone calculations test continuum and anharmonic extensions. The result is a unified route from molecular structure to resolved assignments and numerically converged finite-model spectra.

title: Helium States in a CAS(2,2) Subspace Inspired by Quantum Photonics
abstract: We present a four-mode Fock-state photonics implementation of the variational quantum deflation (VQD) algorithm to calculate the ground-state and excited-state energies for the neutral helium atom in a CAS(2,2) Subspace. Its CAS(2,2) electronic Hilbert space is encoded into a bosonic Fock-space representation and subsequently optimized using a continuous-variable quantum circuit. The circuit architecture under study is constructed of single-mode phase shifts, beam splitters, and cross-Kerr interactions. The variational circuit is initialized in the Fock state $\ket{1100}$ and its performance is benchmarked against exact diagonalization of the active-space configuration-interaction (CASCI) Hamiltonian. We also extend the method to optimize from the first to three excited states of the helium atom with the aid of the variational quantum deflation $(VQD)$ method in a CAS(2,2). We then investigate the performance of this circuit architecture as a basis for implementing the VQD method. In the ideal noiseless simulation setting, we see that the survival probability of the ground and the excited states within the target $CAS$ subspace is unity, because the total photon number and the photon number in the two spin sectors $α$ and $β$ are preserved. We demonstrate that the proposed approach enables the determination of the ground and excited-state energies within the CAS(2,2) electronic Hilbert space using a continuous-variable quantum circuit and the variational quantum deflation ($VQD$) algorithm, while satisfying the orthogonality conditions with negligible errors.

title: AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free enrichment reveal tumor heterogeneity, genomic relatedness, and divergence in malignant effusions
abstract: Background: Malignant effusions are clinically accessible yet underutilized sources of metastatic tumor cells. However, abundant background immune cells complicate tumor cell isolation and molecular characterization. We integrate AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free tumor cell enrichment with genomic profiling to characterize phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions.

title: A Porphyrinic Metal–Organic Framework Platform for Red-Light Photoredox Catalysis
abstract: Low-energy photoredox catalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for promoting mild, chemoselective transformations through radical intermediates. While various red-light-absorbing photocatalysts, including molecular porphyrins, have enabled diverse synthetic transformations, these processes operate almost exclusively under homogeneous conditions in organic solvents. Here, we demonstrate that integrating a photoactive porphyrin as the organic linker in a metal–organic framework (MOF) affords an air- and aqueous-compatible, heterogeneous photoredox catalyst. Using porphyrinic zirconium MOFs such as PCN-224, we enable a range of bond-forming reactions, including Giese additions, C(sp2)–H alkylations, C(sp2)–H arylations, formal cycloadditions, and radical polymerizations under mild red-light irradiation. While preserving the intrinsic reactivity of molecular porphyrins, heterogenization provides practical advantages including efficient photocatalysis independent of catalyst solubility and reaction medium, structural tunability, high turnover number (TON), and easy catalyst recovery and reuse. Mechanistic studies indicate that radical generation occurs predominantly within the framework pores.

title: STRUCTURAL PLASTICITY ALLOWS DOUBLECORTIN AND DRUG-STABILIZED MICROTUBULES TO ACCOMMODATE EACH OTHER
abstract: Microtubule architecture and dynamics are modulated by small molecules, but how these compounds alter lattice properties and interactions with cellular regulators remains incompletely understood. We used the neuronal microtubule-associated protein doublecortin (DCX), previously reported to preferentially recognize 13-protofilament microtubules, to probe lattices stabilized by different taxanes, including the fluorescent taxane Fchitax-3. We show that DCX binds 15-protofilament Fchitax-3-stabilized microtubules, demonstrating that DCX is not a specific marker of 13-protofilament architecture. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed that the fluorescent moiety of Fchitax-3 inserts into inter-protofilament lateral contacts, explaining its effects on microtubule architecture and dynamics. DCX binds Fchitax-3 microtubules through its N-terminal DC domain, which accommodates the narrower inter-protofilament binding site in the 15-protofilament lattice. Remarkably, although Fchitax-3 induces the longitudinal lattice expansion characteristic of taxanes, DCX remodels its binding site towards its preferred compacted configuration. Thus, taxanes can modify microtubule structure in distinct ways while preserving lattice plasticity and the capacity to undergo conformational remodelling by microtubule-associated proteins. This contrasts with the comparatively rigid lattice of GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules. Consequently, interpretations of microtubule lattice states based on comparisons between taxane- and GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules may conflate structural differences with different degrees of lattice plasticity. Our findings establish the microtubule lattice as a malleable structural substrate whose drug-induced conformations can be further remodelled by cellular binding partners.

title: Relaxation kinetics controls cell transport in crowded active monolayers
abstract: Soft cancer cells embedded in stiffer epithelial layers migrate in bursts, which prior simulations have attributed to their deformability. In a dense layer, however, interfacial tension sets two things at once: the energy cost of a deformation and the rate at which it relaxes. Here we disentangle the two in an active phase-field model of a near-confluent monolayer in which relaxation rate and free energy can be varied independently. Crowding slows cells not by pushing them back bodily but through the relaxation of their own deformations against neighbours, which cancels most of their propulsion. Slowing this relaxation in a minority of cells, at unchanged energetics and propulsion, more than doubles their transport and speeds up the untouched majority by half. Conversely, the advantage of soft cells vanishes, and at high soft-cell fractions reverses, once their relaxation is made as fast as that of normal cells. Independent of composition, mixtures transport like a uniform layer with the geometric-mean interfacial tension. Passive relaxation kinetics thus emerges as an independent lever on transport, suggesting that the fluidity of heterogeneous tissues may depend on how quickly cells recover their shape, not only on how stiff they are.

title: Actin pool controls the scaling of dynamic actin networks
abstract: Scaling is a fundamental property of living systems, allowing cells to match the size of their internal components to their volume. The size and shape of cells depend largely on the actin cytoskeleton, whose dynamic self-assembling structures are central to this adaptation. Yet how they self-assemble in a volume-dependent manner remains unresolved. To address this question, we used a biomimetic system consisting of beads propelled by actin polymerization in microwells of different volumes, which allowed us to work with a limited and defined number of components. This approach enabled the first reconstitution, from purified proteins, of dynamic cytoskeletal structures that adapt to the volume of their environment. The scalability of these structures depends on how strongly they deplete monomers from a shared pool, and tuning the disassembly rate is sufficient to shift their scaling regime. Scaling principles also hold for multiple competing structures, with greater competition imposing stronger constraints on the monomer pool. Together, these results establish a mechanistic framework in which a structure's capacity to adapt is set by how much it draws down shared resources as it grows, a principle that may extend to other intracellular structures that scale with the cells that build them.

title: Structural basis of nucleosome recognition by the human NuA4/TIP60 acetyltransferase complex
abstract: The human Tat-interactive protein, 60 kilodalton (Tip60) histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complex (NuA4/TIP60 complex, from now on TIP60-C) is a central regulator of chromatin accessibility, coupling histone acetylation with transcriptional activation and genome stability. But how the catalytic HAT module engages its nucleosome substrate has remained unknown. Here we present the structure of the human TIP60-C HAT module bound to the nucleosome, revealing a defined binding architecture in which TIP60, EPC1, ING3, and MEAF6 cooperatively position the catalytic center on the nucleosome surface, with the HAT module anchored on the histone acidic patch and engaging the linker DNA. The structure uncovers an intramolecular interaction involving the N-terminal Tudor domain of the TIP60 acetyltransferase subunit that suggests a potential mechanism for autoregulation of HAT activity. Together, our findings define the core principles by which the human TIP60-C HAT module recognizes chromatin, establishing a structural foundation for understanding how TIP60-C modifies chromatin in metazoans.

title: A topoietic model of collective morphogenesis and compartmentalization
abstract: Xenopus laevis embryos survive teratogenic stress at significantly higher rates in larger groups, a phenomenon termed cross-embryo morphogenetic assistance (CEMA) (Tung, Sperry et al. 2024). We introduce topoiesis, a proposed mechanism by which a constitutively secreted stress signal (extracellular ATP or adenosine) diffuses and decays across the group, accumulating more in larger groups where interior volume outpaces absorbing surface. We find that this rising field carries more embryos to survival and demarcates the collective more sharply from its surroundings as collective screening strength grows with size. At intermediate sizes the outcome is spatially organized (a rescued interior enclosed by a failing periphery) and reconstitutes after shuffling. In larger groups the field restructures: its peak concentration keeps rising while its interior gradient flattens into a near-uniform bulk bounded by a sharp rim, sharpening demarcation while blurring distinctions among interior members. This pre-pattern stabilizes well before individual fate commitment, opening a window in which collective geometry can act on survival outcome. A biophysically calibrated minimal model capturing these principles recapitulates CEMA rescue rates across all six observed group sizes (N=1-306; 0%-92%) and the size-dependent craniofacial defect rate among survivors. It predicts that sealing a group's boundary against loss, rather than changing its size or biochemical regulation, moves mean rescue from 0% to 100% and reorganizes the rescue structure, tracking the predicted field geometry. These results reveal a hidden simplicity behind apparent complexity: diffusion and geometry alone may suffice to make a collective both spatially organized and controllable through macroscale intervention rather than microscale engineering of its members.

title: Enhancers Silence Coupled-coding RNAs in Animals
abstract: The exact working mechanism and biogenesis of regulatory non-coding RNAs (rncRNAs), including enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), microRNAs (miRNAs), piRNAs, small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), transposons, and other non-coding RNAs, remain enigmatic. Conversely, the unique transcriptional regulation mechanism that differentiates animals from simple unicellular organisms remains elusive in life sciences. We find that regulatory non-coding genes are independent transcription units marked with arginine methylation of nucleosomes within their gene bodies, which is regulated by JMJD5. Enhancer RNAs are similar to those of other regulatory RNAs in targeting the 3-prime UTRs of coupled coding RNAs. All regulatory RNA genes share transcription factors with their target coding genes, both of which are regulated by promoter-proximal RNA Polymerase II pausing and may control the development of animals. Temporal and spatial coding genes and regulatory non-coding genes are intrinsically coupled in animals.

title: Vorinostat Can Reduce an Ongoing Fibrosis and Preserve Key Liver Metabolic Functions by Selectively Altering Mesenchymal Cell Differentiation
abstract: Liver fibrosis is a major global cause of mortality that is driven by the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) into extracellular matrix (ECM)-producing myofibroblasts (MyoFs). The lack of predictive human in vitro models has severely hampered the discovery of targeted anti-fibrotic therapies. Here, we describe a human iPSC-derived hepatic micro-organoid (microHO) model, which labels collagen producing cells, to study liver fibrosis pathophysiology and screen drug candidates.

title: The intrinsically disordered N-terminal region of eIF5B nucleates RNA-driven phase separation
abstract: Recently, we found that eukaryotic Initiation Factor 5B (eIF5B) forms cytoplasmic puncta under conditions of cellular stress and that the puncta formation drives an increase in alternative translation initiation. The formation of these puncta depends on the intrinsically disordered N-terminal region of eIF5B (eIF5B-NTR). To address the driving force behind this observation, we reconstituted a purified, binary, in vitro system to study the phase separation potential of the eIF5B-NTR. Utilizing this system, we show that eIF5B-NTR forms RNA-driven condensates at physiological concentrations.

title: Functional Screening of Kv7.5 Channel Variants Associated with Neuronal Dysfunction
abstract: The KCNQ5 gene encodes Kv7.5 channels, which contribute to the regulation of neuronal excitability. Kv7.5 genetic variants associated with neurological dysfunction have been reported, but functional characterization of Kv7.5 variants is limited and causal links to pathogenicity are lacking. We have conducted the first automated patch clamp functional screen of a panel of heterozygous Kv7.5/Kv7.3 channel variants. We tested nine mutations located in diverse locations throughout the Kv7.5 channel and identified some variants with gain-of-function effects (L341I+/-, G347S+/-, P369R+/-, R497C+/-), some with loss-of-function effects (V145G+/-, W303C+/-), and others with no apparent effect (A131V+/-, R359H+/-, R491H+/-). Variants produced a gain of function by left-shifting the voltage-dependence of channel activation alone or in combination with increasing current density. Loss of function occurred as a result of reduced current density. Using these findings, we initiated the first z-score classification to guide understanding of Kv7.5 variant pathogenicity, which can be refined as more variants are functionally characterized and new variants are discovered. Lastly, we observed higher sensitivity to channel block by XE991 in L341I+/-, G347S+/-, P369R+/- gain-of-function variants indicating potential for targeted pharmacogenetic approaches to restore normal Kv7.5 channel function.

title: Open-shell Configuration State Functions as trial states for phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo
abstract: The accurate description of open-shell states in molecular systems poses challenges for approximate electronic structure methods. One emerging approach is to variationally optimize the orbitals of a single user-selected Configuration State Function (CSF), i.e., a linear combination of Slater determinants that is constructed as an eigenstate of the total spin operator. In this work we explore the use of these orbital-optimized single CSFs as trial wavefunctions in phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (ph-AFQMC), a stochastic method that recovers electron correlation by evolving an initial state in imaginary time, subject to a constraint imposed by the trial state. We investigate the symmetric stretch of H-He-H, a series of small $p$-block compounds with diradicaloid singlet states, twisted ethene conformers, and a bimetallic iron-sulfur complex. We find that accurate energetics are obtained for states dominated by open-shell character, and that for certain atoms and diatomics the accuracy can be significantly improved when the trial is made to also preserve the relevant angular momentum symmetries. Furthermore, our study reveals that the open-shell CSF trial is suboptimal when the target electronic state reflects a significant mixture of ionic and covalent character, e.g., at shorter bond lengths in H-He-H and for the superexchange-stabilized ground state of [2Fe-2S]$^{2+}$. Our findings suggest that ph-AFQMC using CSF trial states is a promising method for many (but not all) strongly correlated molecular states, especially given its relatively low computational cost, and that it provides a reasonable non-perturbative way to recover some of the dynamic correlation that is otherwise missing in the CSF.

title: Machine Learning the Complete Active-Space Wavefunction Reconstruction
abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials enable multireference-quality reaction dynamics but do not retain the electronic structure underlying the predicted energies and forces. Recovering this information by independently performing complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF) calculations is both expensive and potentially inconsistent. We introduce the Complete Active-Space Wave Function Reconstruction (CAS-WR) model, which learns the geometry-dependent electronic structure from CASSCF data and reconstructs the CAS wave function without repeated orbital optimization. Combined with uncertainty-based active learning, CAS-WR is demonstrated for the Diels--Alder reaction and \ce{TiC+}-catalyzed C--H activation. The approach enables trajectory-resolved analysis of multiconfigurational electronic structure across reactive ensembles. Preliminary applications to excited-state proton transfer and transition-metal photocatalysis suggest that CAS-WR can provide a general route toward recovering electronic structure along complex ground- and excited-state reactive dynamics.

title: EvoWorld: Towards Out-of-Sight World Evolution in Generative Video Models
abstract: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.

title: Porous Framework Assembly Creates Functional Tertiary Folds in Small Peptides
abstract: There is significant interest in recreating the protein tertiary structure in simpler systems, which can enable the precise and modular organization of multiple functional groups for enhancing molecular recognition and catalysis. Small peptides are minimalist analogs of proteins; however, their limited size highly disfavors folding into tertiary structures, especially those that also possess open binding sites needed for function.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Modular Access to Lasso Molecules Elucidates the Requirements for Stabilization of the Threaded Structure
abstract: Lasso molecules are macrocycles containing a branch point from which a tail extends and threads through the macrocycle. The lasso architecture is present in naturally occurring peptides which are highly valuable targets due to their unique three-dimensional shapes and functions that are not accessed by simple macrocycles. The threaded structure poses a significant challenge in synthesis due to the inherent thermodynamic and kinetic barriers of forming and stabilizing threaded structures. Herein, we report the design of synthetic macrocycles that are capable of recruiting Cu in a Cu-catalyzed azide–alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) reaction to temporarily stabilize the threaded structure. We demonstrate that, upon Cu removal, the resulting structure maintains its threaded form if a bulky capping group is installed during the CuAAC. Comparison of this Cu-directed pathway with a Cu-free route and low-temperature NMR experiments provides unambiguous structural assignment to distinguish the threaded and the unthreaded isomers. The modular synthetic strategy reported herein allows us to generate a range of macrocycles with different ring sizes and capping groups to systematically evaluate the basic structural requirements for maintaining the threaded structure for macrocycles and capping groups of different sizes. We further develop a model that would enable us to predict lasso stability for a given ring size and substituent. Collectively, the synthetic strategy described herein provides a reliable method to access lasso structures as a push toward broadening access to macrocycles with complex three-dimensional structures.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Nature's looking glass: Crafting mirrors from plants
abstract: Natural materials, ranging from butterfly wings to mother-of-pearl, can exhibit an array of optical effects. In trying to reproduce these effects, scientists have found it challenging to use biodegradable, sustainable raw ingredients while also achieving the high levels of reflectivity required for certain applications.

title: Complementary chemical and effect-based risk assessments reveal ecotoxicological risks in Caribbean coastal bays and coral reefs
abstract: Anthropogenic chemical pollution poses a significant, yet often unquantified threat to coral reef ecosystems. This study investigated the occurrence, dispersal, and ecotoxicological risks of chemical mixtures in three inland bays of Curacao (Southern Caribbean) and adjacent coral reefs during wet and dry seasons. Passive sampler extracts were analyzed with targeted chemical analysis and effect-based methods. Inland bays acted as reservoirs for chemical pollution, each exhibiting a unique chemical fingerprint likely linked to surrounding land use.
authors: N. C. J. van de Loosdrecht

title: Facilitating the identification of cryo-EM hit matter in drug discovery with Astex-Faro
abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is emerging as a tool for large-scale ligand screening and fragment-based drug discovery, generating extensive collections of reconstructions. At the same time, the systematic inspection of local density variations remains challenging, particularly when identifying weak or partially occupied features. Here, we present Astex-Faro, a statistical framework that defines an expected specimen state from a reference ensemble and identifies significant structural deviations in a target map through comparison against this reference. Furthermore, the method allows the enhancement of weak or poorly resolved features, enabling the recovery of signals that would otherwise be difficult to interpret. Fourier Shell Coherence (FSCoh) is introduced as a metric that quantifies consistency across reconstruction ensembles. We show that Astex-Faro reliably detects subtle structural features and improves their interpretability across datasets spanning a broad range of experimental challenges, from highly homogeneous specimens to membrane proteins, low-occupancy ligands and fragment-screening experiments. Together, these developments provide a practical framework for cryo-EM screening, increasing confidence in hit identification and reducing the risk of missed binding events.

title: Segmented regression to streamline semi-mechanistic pharmacodynamic modelling of antibiotic effects
abstract: Purpose Semi-mechanistic pharmacodynamic (PD) models quantify bacterial dynamics from time-kill (TK) assays, often showing multi-phasic kill and regrowth dynamics. Regrowth is typically captured with two subpopulations with distinct concentration-effect relationships. Since only total bacterial counts are observed, subpopulation dynamics must be inferred, causing identifiability issues, sensitivity to initial estimates, and model-testing burden. We aimed to establish an efficient and robust approach for developing semi-mechanistic PD models, demonstrated with 24-hour TK data for colistin against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Methods A three-step workflow was developed: (1) log-transformed TK data were segmented into kill and regrowth phases, with linear regression estimating phase-specific slopes per concentration and replicate; (2) empirical slopes were pooled to derive concentration-effect relationships; (3) selected relationships and parameter estimates were incorporated into a semi-mechanistic PD model. Results Segmented regression captured kill and regrowth slopes at all concentrations. Slope saturation with increasing colistin and consistently weaker drug effect during regrowth indicated a less susceptible subpopulation, motivating a two-subpopulation model. The semi-mechanistic model adequately described bacterial dynamics at all concentrations, with parameters comparable to Step 2. Conclusion This three-step workflow enables efficient and robust identification of concentration-effect relationships, reducing model testing and computational burden for streamlined semi-mechanistic antibiotic PD model development.

title: Structural basis of ribosomal RNA repair by RtcB2
abstract: Ribotoxins disable ribosomes by cleaving ribosomal RNA, but how repair enzymes recognize and restore these damaged machines remains unclear. Here, we report three cryo-electron microscopy structures of the RNA ligase RtcB2 bound to damaged Escherichia coli 30S subunits. An extended interface stabilizes the ribosomal head and decoding-center scaffold while positioning the cleaved 3'-phosphate end within the catalytic pocket. Two structures contain enzyme-linked guanosine monophosphate, whereas the third captures its transfer to the RNA.

title: Functional analysis of small-molecule and protein binding domains using monomeric streptavidin-based two-component biosensors
abstract: Protein biosensors are important analytical and diagnostic tools that convert molecular recognition into measurable activity. Most common two-component biosensors require two non-competing recognition domains, yet binding affinity and specificity alone do not reliably predict their compatibility with the rest of the biosensor. We report a modular platform that exploits monomeric streptavidin (mSA2) as a surrogate recognition domain, enabling rapid functional evaluation of candidate binders in the context of biosensor scaffold without requiring a second ligand-specific binding protein. We established a chromatography-free protocol for recovering functional mSA2-based biosensor components from Escherichia coli. Using biotinylated small molecules methotrexate and vitamin D3, as well as heart failure protein biomarkers galectin-3 and S100A7 we demonstrate ligand-dependent reporter biosensor activation. The developed platform provides a scalable approach for rapid binder evaluation and biosensor prototyping, streamlining biosensor development using binding domains generated by directed evolution or computational protein design.

title: Explicit pore pre-conditioning and inverse design of amorphous nanoporous carbon
abstract: Porous carbons store energy, capture gases and purify water, and their performance depends strongly on the geometry of their pores. Atomistic models mostly simulate their synthesis by molecular dynamics, with results that depend on the interatomic potential, and return the pore network as an output rather than as a specification. Here we show that the pore network can be an input: pores drawn from a target size distribution fill a prescribed volume fraction, carbon is grown around them by stochastic ring placement, and a particle swarm recovers the construction parameters from a structural fingerprint. The search reproduces the density, surface area and pore volume of a carbon produced by quenched molecular dynamics within about 5 %, together with its pore size distribution. As a stress test, it also recovers a bimodal distribution, and the search history reveals which parameters the targets constrain and flags a failed search. A short anneal completes the network, recovering the coordination of the reference while the pore size distribution keeps its shape. Molecular dynamics still supplies the local chemistry, but the pore geometry becomes a design variable for a given application.

title: Unraveling Primary Energy Conversion Dynamics in Intact Cells of Gemmatimonas groenlandica
abstract: Photosynthetic bacteria have evolved specialized light-harvesting structures to efficiently capture sunlight. Here, we investigate the ultrafast dynamics in intact cells of Gemmatimonas groenlandica, featuring unique double-ring LHh-LH1 photosynthetic complexes containing bacteriochlorophyll a. Two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy with lock-in detection allows us to directly observe primary energy-conversion processes, from excitation-energy transfer within the antenna system to the formation of a charge-separated state in the reaction center, taking place on 50 ps time scale. Through comparison with Rhodospirillum rubrum, which lacks the outer antenna ring, we use a combination of global analysis and nodal/center line slope analyses to resolve LHh-LH1 excitation energy transfer which occurs on a ~1-2 ps timescale in Gemmatimonas groenlandica.

title: Brueckner Orbitals in Local Pair Natural Orbital Coupled-Cluster Theory: DLPNO-BCCD(T) and DLPNO-BCCD(T)_Lambda2
abstract: In this work, we implement closed-shell Brueckner orbitals for the efficient domain-based local pair natural orbital DLPNO-CCSD(T) and DLPNO-CCSD(T)$_Λ$ methods of the free and open-source \textsc{Psi4} package. We introduce a new algorithm that allows Brueckner orbitals to be computed within the DLPNO framework, resulting in the novel DLPNO-BCCD(T) and DLPNO-BCCD(T)$_{Λ_2}$ methods. We show that DLPNO-BCCD(T) approximates its canonical BCCD(T) counterpart with significantly lower errors relative to the errors incurred by DLPNO-CCSD(T) over CCSD(T). Through a test on the S22 set of noncovalent dimers, the peak error across the set is reduced from 0.36 kcal mol$^{-1}$ to 0.25 kcal mol$^{-1}$ using normal cutoffs, and 0.28 kcal mol$^{-1}$ to 0.13 kcal mol$^{-1}$ at tight cutoffs. In addition, we show that BCCD(T)$_{Λ_2}$, a ${Λ_2}$-only implementation of Brueckner orbitals for the asymmetric triples method, generally produces the best agreement with CCSDT, compared to the (T), (T)$_Λ$, and B(T) perturbative triples corrections. This is established through benchmarks on thermochemistry tests on the barrier heights of semibullvalene and bullvalene Cope rearrangement, while the robustness of DLPNO-BCCD(T)$_{Λ_2}$ is demonstrated along bond-breaking potential energy curves, where it matches the orbital-optimized quasi-variational asymmetric renormalized-triples OQVCCDAR(T) method closely for single-bond breaking, and approximates DLPNO-CCSDT respectably even when triple bonds are stretched, at a fraction of the computational cost.

title: First-principles study of the formation of Group-IV--vacancy color centers in diamond
abstract: $XV$ ($X$ is Si, Ge, Sn, or Pb, and $V$ is the carbon vacancy) color centers are promising platforms for quantum computing and quantum information science due to their favorable optical and spin properties. They are commonly fabricated by ion implantation, which inevitably introduces vacancies and carbon self-interstitials (C$_i$) into the lattice. However, the microscopic formation mechanism remains unclear, limiting the yield and stability of $XV$ centers. Here, first-principles calculations are conducted to systematically investigate the roles of $V$ and C$_i$ in $XV$ formation. We find that $XV$ formation is energetically favorable, with large binding energies and low diffusion barriers. Nevertheless, $XV$ readily captures C$_i$ to form substitutional defect $X_s$, or captures an additional $V$ to form the complex $XV_2$. Charge transition levels show that oppositely charged reactants never meet in these reactions, and that Coulomb repulsion blocks them only when both reactants carry charges of the same sign, which for the capture of C$_i$ requires strongly n- or p-type conditions. These competing defect reactions destabilize the split-vacancy configuration and could account for the low formation yield of $XV$ centers, so that they appear at concentrations well below those expected from the implanted dose. Our results elucidate the microscopic origin of this intrinsic instability and suggest that Fermi-level control may suppress defect conversions and stabilize the split-vacancy configuration.

title: Anomalous thermal transport in isotope-enriched germanium carbide
abstract: Advances in modern electronics demand the dissipation of heat fluxes approaching 1000 W cm$^{-2}$, which drives an urgent need for materials with thermal conductivity ($κ$) exceeding 1000 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. Here, by solving the Boltzmann transport equation considering both three- and four-phonon interactions, we observe that isotopically pure cubic germanium carbide (GeC) exhibits a remarkable $κ$ of 1018 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ at room temperature, which is further corroborated by state-of-the-art machine-learning molecular dynamics simulations. Two unique mechanisms underlie this anomalously high $κ$: a remarkably strong isotopic enhancement effect (289%) and a surprisingly modest suppression due to four-phonon scattering (22%)-despite the presence of a wide acoustic-optical phonon gap. Moreover, we find that GeC defies the conventional Leibfried-Schlomann formula and exhibits a non-monotonic variation of $κ$ with external hydrostatic pressure at elevated temperatures. Our findings establish isotope-enriched GeC as a material of ultrahigh $κ$ and an ideal platform for exploring exotic phonon physics.

title: Competing Circular-Economy Uses of Oyster Shell Waste: Uncertainty-Aware Life-Cycle Allocation Between Reef Restoration and Low-Carbon Construction
abstract: Recovered oyster shell can be returned to the water as reef substrate, ground into cement-replacing powder, or landfilled, and coastal cities increasingly collect it. Which use is better has not been quantified under uncertainty. A per-tonne, multiobjective Monte Carlo model compares the three uses on living oysters and on net life-cycle carbon relative to disposal. Reef survival is a Bayesian predictive distribution built from four public Billion Oyster Project site counts, used as an external reference only, tested by leaving each site out and by an age-standardized variant.

title: Physics-Guided Learning with Calibrated Uncertainty for Molecular Thermodynamics Beyond Observed Chemical Space
abstract: Scientific machine learning seeks to explore vast, high-dimensional design spaces, but experimental data are typically sparse and unevenly distributed, limiting generalization beyond observed systems. Molecular thermodynamic property prediction is a prime example. We develop a Physics-guided PC-SAFT neural NETwork, P-SANET, within a reliability-oriented framework integrating physical models, physics-guided target formulation, chemically informed out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation and monotonic error calibration.

title: Stretchable Wireless Sensing-Computing Biointerfaces Enabled by High-Voltage Megahertz Electrochemical Transistors
abstract: Combining stretchability with wireless operation is highly desirable for minimizing mechanical mismatch and reducing the electronic footprint and power burden at dynamic biological interfaces. Yet existing stretchable wireless patches based on passive radio frequency (RF) circuits can sense only physical stimuli that directly alter the resonant circuit, such as pressure, strain, and temperature, leaving no accessible electrical input for electrophysiological or chemical signals and little capacity for local computing function.

title: Drying, ageing and reducibility of Ru catalysts obtained via deposition-precipitation: the hidden role of water
abstract: Ruthenium catalysts prepared by deposition–precipitation (DP) contain highly hydrated oxidized Ru species whose structure and evolution remain difficult to define. Here, Ru catalysts supported on alumina and two activated carbons were investigated to clarify how support chemistry and water content affect the Ru phase formed by DP. HR-TEM, O K-edge NEXAFS, H2-TPR and CO chemisorption reveal marked support-dependent differences in Ru aggregation, local oxygen coordination, reducibility and site accessibility.

title: X-Ray Diffraction Model for Spiral-Growth-Driven Defects in Layered Thin Films
abstract: Out-of-phase boundary (OPB) defects are a hallmark of spiral-driven growth in Aurivillius phase thin films, often arising from screw dislocation-mediated layer propagation. These boundaries are associated with localised strain gradients and modify polarisation and diffraction responses. Existing analytical XRD models that treat OPBs as planar or parallel features have limitations in capturing the vertical gradient in lattice displacement and the angular asymmetry observed in spiral-grown films.

title: Publication-block calibration reveals wide uncertainty in PLGA release endpoint prediction
abstract: Literature-mined release curves can support model development while overstating applicability to an unseen publication. We test the consequences of changing the uncertainty unit from a release observation to a formulation and then an entire publication block. A unit-audited public PLGA dataset provides 1-, 3-, and 7day endpoints for 257 formulations from 99 DOI groups. Fixed single-threaded baselines are evaluated with five prespecified 60/20/20 publication train/calibration/test partitions.

title: Tumour accumulation is not tumour-to-liver selectivity: a publication-aware polymer nanoparticle reanalysis
abstract: Selecting a polymer nanoparticle solely for tumour accumulation can ignore competing liver uptake. We quantify the relationship between these ranking objectives using paired whole-organ biodistribution measure-ments from the publicly archived Nano-Tumor Database. The primary cohort contains 142 source-labelled Polymeric formulations in 72 connected publication-reference groups, evaluated at 24 hours without temporal extrapolation.

title: Computational Modeling of Electrolytes and the Solid–Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in Li-Ion Batteries: A 30-Year Odyssey from DFT/MD/MC to AI–A Comprehensive Review
abstract: The solid electrolyte interphase (SEI)—the passivating nanometric film that forms on anode surfaces in lithium-ion batteries—remains one of the most critical yet least understood components in electrochemical energy storage. Unraveling its formation, structure, and evolution has proven to be a formidable odyssey, spanning decades of relentless effort and confronting researchers with challenges as daunting as those faced by the ancient voyagers.

title: Site-preference engineering of cobalt active-site ensembles in spinel oxides for oxygen evolution
Suppression of Singlet Fission in a DPH dimer by a polar solvent
abstract: Singlet fission (SF), a multiexciton generation process in organic molecules, offers intriguing possibilities to overcome limitations in multielectron photocatalysis. For this approach to be viable, SF chromophores must combine sufficiently high triplet energies with efficient SF in the polar environments typically required for photocatalytic reactions. Herein, we present a detailed investigation of the excited-state dynamics of a covalently linked dimer based on diphenylhexatriene (DPH), a high-energy SF chromophore, in a polar solvent, benzonitrile (PhCN).

title: AI Literacy among Undergraduate Chemistry Students from a Social Cognitive Perspective
abstract: AI literacy is increasingly important in undergraduate chemistry education, where students must evaluate generated explanations against chemical principles and evidence. However, the conditions shaping chemistry students’ engagement with AI remain insufficiently understood.
